groups.title: JavaScript Core Mechanics
groups.question: Explain how JavaScript runs async code on a single thread, and how functions keep access to outside variables.

followUps.The Event Loop & Microtask Queue: Why might a Promise callback run before a setTimeout callback with a delay of zero?
followUps.Closures & Lexical Scope: Why can a closure keep a large object in memory longer than you expect?

evidence.text: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time; async callbacks wait in queues until the current code finishes.
After the current code, all promise callbacks (microtasks) run before the next timer or I/O callback.
So a resolved promise's callback runs before a setTimeout with zero delay.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (event loop, microtask, macrotask) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says callbacks run on several threads, or that setTimeout with zero delay always runs first.

evidence.text: A function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was defined, even after that outer function has returned.
It holds references to those variables, not copies.
So anything the closure references, like a big object, stays in memory as long as the closure is reachable, for example from a listener or timer.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (closure, lexical scope) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a closure copies the variables and frees them when the outer function returns.

groups.title: TypeScript for Backend
groups.question: Walk through how you use TypeScript to keep a Node.js backend type safe.

followUps.Generics & Type Narrowing: How does narrowing a union type help you avoid runtime errors in an API handler?
followUps.tsconfig for Node.js: Why can a Node.js TypeScript project compile cleanly and still fail on imports at runtime?

evidence.text: Generics let one function or type work with many types while keeping the specific type, instead of falling back to any.
Narrowing checks a value at runtime (typeof, in, or a tag field) so TypeScript knows which member of a union it is.
After narrowing you can't touch a field that only exists on another shape, which prevents runtime errors in a handler.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (generics, type narrowing, union types) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says TypeScript checks types at runtime, so request input doesn't need validating.

evidence.text: The compiler checks types, not whether the emitted imports will actually load in Node.
If the module settings don't match how Node loads the project (CommonJS vs ESM, file extensions), it compiles but fails at runtime.
module and moduleResolution have to match the Node setup, for example node16 or nodenext.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (tsconfig, module, moduleResolution) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says code that compiles without errors will always run.
